keyVerseText: And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt. to destroy: Heb. for a destruction
rootMeaning: The root of מַשְׁחִית (mashchîyth) is שָׁחַת (shâchath), which conveys the idea of decay, ruin, and destruction both literally and figuratively. This root emphasizes a process of corruption or spoiling, not merely physical destruction but also moral or systemic decay. Thus, מַשְׁחִית carries a sense of active destruction or ruin that goes beyond simple damage, involving a comprehensive undoing or wasting.
usageInScripture: Throughout its 11 occurrences, מַשְׁחִית is consistently associated with destruction, ruin, or corruption, whether physical, moral, or figurative. It appears in contexts describing traps, utter ruin, and divine judgment, as seen in translations like 'to destroy,' 'a trap,' and 'of corruption.' This range shows the word's flexibility in describing both tangible and intangible forms of destruction, underscoring the severity and totality of the ruin it denotes.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַשְׁחִית deepens our grasp of the biblical portrayal of sin and judgment as comprehensive destruction that affects both body and soul. It reveals the seriousness with which God views corruption and ruin, highlighting His holiness against the backdrop of human sinfulness. This word reminds believers of the reality of divine judgment but also points to the need for redemption through Christ, who conquers destruction and corruption. It calls the faithful to live in the hope of restoration, knowing that ultimate ruin is met by God's sovereign mercy.
keyVerseReflection: In Exodus 12:13, the term מַשְׁחִית is rendered as 'to destroy,' emphasizing the plague's deadly threat on Egypt. The verse highlights the protective power of the blood on the houses of the Israelites, which causes the plague 'not to be upon you to destroy you.' Here, מַשְׁחִית stresses the totality of the destruction from which God delivers His people, illustrating His power to save from utter ruin and judgment.
